blocks.text: My toy boat sat still all winter, so I opened its tiny motor to find out what makes it spin.
Inside, two things: a curved magnet and a copper coil. Send electricity through the wire, and the coil becomes a magnet too!
Picture it from inside: opposite poles pull, matching poles push, so the coil swings a half turn, then stops, stuck.
The trick is this split ring, the commutator. Every half turn it flips the current, so the coil's poles swap and it keeps chasing!
I tucked the motor back into its hull and wired it up, then waited weeks for the frozen pond to thaw.
Then came the first warm day. Push, pull, flip, repeat, thousands of times a minute, and my boat raced across the pond.

blocks.text: Every summer morning, Hazel walks the edge of the wildflower meadow, peering under leaves. Today, beneath a milkweed leaf, she finds a secret no bigger than a pinhead.
This is a monarch butterfly egg. Its mother chose milkweed on purpose, because it's the only kind of plant her caterpillars will eat. Clever mum, really.
A few days later, a tiny caterpillar chews its way out. Its very first meal is its own eggshell. Then it turns to the milkweed, and simply never stops.
Over two weeks it eats and grows, shedding its skin again and again as it outgrows it. By the end, it's about two thousand times heavier than when it hatched.
If I grew like that, I'd be as heavy as a car. And caterpillars do almost nothing but eat. Honestly, I find that rather relatable.
One afternoon it stops eating and crawls off; Hazel follows it to the meadow's hawthorn hedge. There it spins a silk button, hooks on, and hangs in a letter J.
Its skin splits one final time. Underneath isn't another caterpillar, but a smooth green case dotted with gold. This is the chrysalis, and inside, something astonishing begins.
Here's the surprising part. Inside, the caterpillar releases digestive juices that break down much of its own body into a kind of living soup. Not quite a nap, then.
But not everything dissolves. Tiny clusters of cells, tucked away since before the caterpillar even hatched, feed on that soup and build wings, legs, antennae and eyes.
Scientists have even found hints that some moths remember lessons learned as caterpillars. So perhaps a little of the old self survives the soup. Lovely thought.
After about ten days, the case turns clear, showing folded orange wings. Then the butterfly pushes out, crumpled and damp, clinging on while its wings slowly unfurl.
It pumps fluid into its wing veins until they stretch flat, rests a few hours to dry, then lifts away. Same creature, completely remade.

blocks.text: High in California's White Mountains, the air is thin, the soil is bone-dry, and the wind never stops. Nothing up here hurries. Especially not me.

Meanwhile, the world below kept changing. Rome rose and fell. Great cathedrals went up. Ships crossed oceans. And up here, one ring a year, Methuselah simply kept growing.
